content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a generalized acquisition function for Bayesian optimization (BO) called h-entropy search. The acquisition function is defined as expected reduction of the loss function for which connection with the entropy is shown by existing studies. The authors discuss that h-entropy search includes several well-known acquisition functions as a special case. For three application scenarios, examples of the loss function definitions are shown, for which empirical evaluations are also provided.
content.main_review:
The paper is easy to follow and well-organized. The application examples would be useful. However, technical novelty of the paper is limited. Although the authors emphasize generality of the proposed framework, I do not see significance for the generality because it does not provide novel acquisition function for the usual BO and no properties that hold commonly for each one of special cases are revealed. It is seemingly no more that that equations can be written by a common representation. The three application examples are practically interesting, the proposed approach is a simple expected risk reduction, by which novelty for the design of acquisition function is somewhat marginal. Detailed comments are as follows.

As the authors mentioned, h-entropy can be seen as a generalized formula of a various criteria such as EI, ES, and KG. However, I do not think that just deriving a generalized formulation is significant. If there exist some 'shared' statistical property in the context of BO such as convergence rate, it is worth generalizing different criteria. The paper does not reveal any shared property of each one of special cases. In this sense, I'd have to say that the connection is superficial. Although there exist several existing studies for connection between h-entropy and information, their context is quite general and implications for BO and GP are not clarified. 

Why can (2) be 'entropy' (i.e., amount of information)? This is essential, but nothing is discussed. The authors just refer the existing studies, and do not justify the interpretation that it is still an effective way to measure the information gain in the context of BO.

Related to that, although the h-entropy is proposed as an uncertainty measure, can it always be seen as an uncertainty measure regardless of the definition of the loss \ell? For example, KG only evaluates the change of the posterior mean. This indicate that even when there still exists a large amount of uncertainty, KG can have better value if the posterior mean is improved, compared with other options that reduce uncertainty a lot though the posterior mean is not improved. This is another reason that I thought the connection is only superficial.

Particularly in three application examples, the proposed framework simply evaluate a difference of the expected performance between the current and the one step ahead models. In my understanding, it is a kind of the classical expected error reduction (EER) in active learning. The EER is a reasonable strategy, but I do not think that designing EER for specific tasks has particular technical significance.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper is well-organized with good application scenarios, technical novelty of the proposed framework is not satisfactory.

content.title: Response to Reviewer YEC3
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments and feedback. We will use these to improve the quality of our paper. We respond back to your comments below.

###  **Benefits of a general representation:**
We think you bring up a nice discussion on the topic of *why* it is beneficial to develop our general framework, which both unifies existing acquisition functions (EI, ES/PES, KG), and can specialize to more general tasks beyond simple optimization.

Our main motivation in developing this framework was for the following reasons:
1. It is often unclear which of the existing acquisition functions to use in a given run of BO; our framework provides explicit guidance of when it is more optimal to choose e.g. EI vs ES/PES vs KG, depending on a user’s goals, and the loss that they care about (see “Practical guidance and summary” in Section 4).
2. Our framework allows for easily and automatically deriving one-step-optimal acquisition procedures for new optimization problems given a specific user-provided loss (and we demonstrate this on three example tasks).
3. Our framework allows for gradient-based acquisition optimization methods on a wide set of tasks—both for new acquisition functions, as well as on existing acquisition functions such as KG/ES (and this in turn can yield new procedures for existing BO acquisition functions).

We will state these reasons more explicitly in an updated draft of our paper.

### **Why can (2) be viewed as entropy and (3) as information gain:**
After reading your comments, we agree that addition discussion and intuition is merited when we define the H-entropy and H-information gain (EHIG). We provide some clarification below, and will add this discussion to our paper:

H-entropy $H_\ell[X] = \inf_a \mathbb{E}[\ell(X, a)]$ is a natural notion of uncertainty because it is the Bayes optimal loss of a decision maker who must select some action $a$ not for a particular $x$, but in expectation for a random $X$. Intuitively, whenever the decision maker is uncertain about $X$, she is less able to choose an action to minimize the loss, so a higher loss indicates more uncertainty. In addition, by choosing specific loss functions, H-entropy recovers many common uncertainty measures in the literature, such as the Shannon entropy when $\ell$ is the log loss, and the variance when $\ell$ is the quadratic loss. 

Correspondingly, the reduction in H-entropy is a natural notion of information, similar to how Shannon information is the reduction of Shannon entropy. Concretely, H-entropy reduction measures the reduction in the Bayes optimal loss of a decision maker after new observations. Intuitively, it measures the “useful” information that can be used to choose better actions to reduce loss. In the context of BO, our goal is to make the most “useful” query that helps us choose better actions (e.g. the top-k points or the level set), hence H-entropy reduction is a natural acquisition function to achieve this.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1668 by Reviewer NMWE

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors showed that existing BO methods are special cases of different loss functions in H-entropy / information gain. Using H-entropy/information gain, the authors were able to derive a series of new acquisition functions and their gradient based optimization methods for problems including subset selection and level set estimation.
content.main_review:
I really liked this paper when I read the abstract, and I think it indeed proposed interesting ideas on H-entropy to connect different concepts related to Bayesian optimization. However, I found it a bit disappointing that the writing is not clear and some basic definitions are somewhat confusing.

1. There are a couple of places where writing can be much improved in the introduction.
1.1 It was not clear to me whether the focus is on introducing H entropy to address more tasks (including level set estimation etc) or to make connections among different acquisition functions. It was not until the end of the intro where I start to realize that both are proposed. It just doesn't feel crystal clear what exactly the authors are trying to propose. For example, 2nd paragraph is all talking about different tasks other than BO, but the title is about BO. And then 4th paragraph started talking about BO again but just 1 sentence, then it's back to other tasks. Reading the intro makes me feel like the author who wrote the intro did not have a clear mind.
1.2 The choices of words make it very confusing. I would not call level set estimation an optimization task. As far as I know, BO and Bayesian level set estimation are usually considered "siblings" rather than "parent-children". The same for top k with diversity: that is subset selection.
1.3 Contributions can be made clearer: the last two points seem to be one. Also what is a strong empirical performance? Can you be more concrete?

2. Related to Setup and Experiments: though I understand that the loss term is defined to facilitate the definitions of H entropy and information gain, I don't think it's necessary to introduce loss as l=-f(x*) and then in experiments evaluate -l as the metric, which is basically f(x*). To me, it is very confusing. Can you define H entropy instead for a maximizing objective such as f(x*)?

3. Under the definition of H entropy, can you include some discussions on how it is related to regular definitions of entropy, e.g. Shannon, Rényi etc? Proposition 2 has the related proof but it happens much later in the paper. I think it's also good to explain in detail which definition/theorem in which paper introduced this Definition 1 and add its citation properly at Definition 1. I briefly looked through the cited papers but didn't find anything similar to what the authors defined. I do wonder whether Definition 1 should be called entropy, which evaluates how "chaotic" a distribution is. If Definition 1 is novel, I think the definition of a newly proposed entropy is beyond the expertise of this conference and should be reviewed by the mathematics and probability community.

4. I would suggest having more intuitions on what H entropy/information gain implies and how choosing a loss function could impact H entropy. In particular, for entropy search, what exactly does distribution q mean?

5. While these acquisition functions can be interpreted as H information gain with different losses, how does this understanding help us choosing a better loss function?

6. Is multi-value sequence search a new problem? If not, please add citations for it.

7. What is the runtime or complexity of the proposed method? It seems to me that the gradient can be expensive to compute given the optimization steps for each gradient.

8. There are a lot of tasks discussed in this work but there is not enough space for experiments that demonstrate and analyze the performance of methods for different benchmarks in each task. The baseline methods are also very limited. For level set estimation, there are existing simple methods that work well https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2005/hash/8e930496927757aac0dbd2438cb3f4f6-Abstract.html. For subset selection (or what the authors call top k estimation with diversity), at the very least one can compare to classic work such as https://jmlr.org/papers/volume9/krause08a/krause08a.pdf. I'm also confused how KG, as a BO method, is selected to solve LSE and subset selection problems.

9. Is H-entropy/information gain submodular?
content.summary_of_the_review: The overall ideas on H-entropy and its interpretations for BO methods are very interesting. However the writing is not very clear and experiments are lacking. I hope the authors can address the issues to make the paper more readable and convincing.

content.title: Response to Reviewer NMWE
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments, feedback, and questions. We will use these to improve the quality of our paper. We respond back to each comment below.

### **Emphasis in the introduction:**
We understand your point here—thanks for bringing it up. It seems like there are a couple of points that we need to clarify:
1. You are correct that we do want to accomplish two goals with our framework: (a) unify existing acquisition functions and (b) easily/automatically derive acquisition functions for new tasks given a user-supplied loss.
2. You bring up that “optimization” (or even “generalized optimization”) is not a good term for some of the tasks that our framework applies to — such as level-set estimation, top-k estimation/subset selection, sequence search, etc.

We think a lot of the confusion in our intro probably stems from bullet #2 above. In our minds, we viewed these other, specialized tasks as “generalized optimization” (as you said: a type of “child”, or perhaps *extension* of optimization, rather than a “sibling”). Given this, some of the back-and-forth shifts that you had described in our intro come from this distinction, because in our minds we were conflating BO with these other extension tasks.

That being said, we think you bring up a nice point that this is not clear, and probably not the best terminology to use. Instead, we will update our intro so that we do not refer to these other tasks as “optimization”. We will also make it clear early-on in the intro that we have two goals: (a) provide benefits to existing acquisition functions for optimization (e.g. relations between them, guidance on when to select one over another, new acquisition optimization methods); and (b) easily/automatically derive acquisition functions for other, related tasks, given a user-supplied loss.

### **Further details and intuition on H-entropy, EHIG:**
Thanks for this feedback. To clarify here: our definition of H-entropy is *not* novel, and in the prior work that we cited ([1] page 408, equation 2.14; [2] page 69, equation 2.1-2.2; [3] page 1375, equation 12) is defined as either a generalized entropy or an “H entropy”. We agree that we should point out these equations explicitly, and provide some more intuition about the definition (and relation to e.g. Shannon, Reyni entropies, near this definition) — we will make this update in our paper.

[1] M H DeGroot. Uncertainty, information, and sequential experiments. Ann. Math. Stat., 33(2): 404–419, 1962.

[2] C R Rao. Convexity properties of entropy functions and analysis of diversity. Lecture Notes-Monograph Series, pp. 68–77, 1984.

[3] P D Grünwald and A P Dawid. Game theory, maximum entropy, minimum discrepancy and robust bayesian decision theory. Ann. Stat., 32(4):1367–1433, 2004.

### **Runtime complexity:**
We will add timing results to our paper. As an example, we performed a timing study on the top-k estimation problem, and our method takes between 3s and 10s per iteration (depending on the stage of the trial and number of observations). This is similar to the time taken by baselines such as knowledge gradient (KG).

### **Help in choosing a loss:**
The motivation for our framework is the following: suppose a user has a specific problem (be it optimization, or a sibling task) and a loss that they care about; we aim to then provide a one-step-optimal acquisition function tailored to this task—and an efficient acquisition optimization algorithm. For existing BO acquisition functions, our framework provides explicit guidance on which acquisition function to choose, based on what the user cares about (i.e. what loss they have); we give this guidance in Section 4 (“Practical guidance and summary” section). For new acquisition functions for other tasks, our framework similarly aims to provides an acquisition procedure that is tailored to a given user-supplied loss.

### **Submodularity:**
We have not yet studied the submodularity of EHIG, but we agree that it is an interesting direction for future study.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces H-entropy search, a family of acquisition functions (AFs) for Bayesian optimization (BO) built on the concept of H-entropy, a generalization of the classical Shannon entropy. An H-entropy is determined by a loss function, $\ell$, and a set of actions, $\mathcal{A}$. The choice of  $\ell$ and $\mathcal{A}$ can be tailored to an arbitrary quantity of interest to minimize. Thus, this approach does not only provide a flexible family of AFs for standard BO but also for other related problems such as level set estimation. Moreover, it is shown that many widely used AFs in standard BO can be derived as special cases of this family of acquisition functions under suitable choices of $\ell$ and $\mathcal{A}$. It is also shown that, under suitable conditions, this type of AF is differentiable and its gradients can be computed using an infinitesimal perturbation analysis, thus allowing the use of gradient-based methods for a more efficient AF optimization. Finally, several numerical experiments under various choices of $\ell$ and $\mathcal{A}$ are conducted, showing favorable results compared to other existing methods.
content.main_review:
Strengths

1. This work introduces an interesting unified view of various BO AFs through the lenses of H-entropy measures.
2. The realistic test problems considered in this work are interesting and, to my knowledge, novel within the BO literature.

Weaknesses

This paper has multiple weaknesses that I describe in detail below.

1. While the H-entropy search family of AFs is interesting in that it encompasses many of the existing acquisition functions for BO, its usefulness is not clearly demonstrated (and is not evident to me). This family of AFs is so broad that deriving general theoretical results or efficient computational methods for it seems very challenging. As an example of this, the conditions under which the differentiability of these AFs is proved are not satisfied by the knowledge gradient or entropy search AFs.

2. The formulations provided for the top-k estimation and multi-value sequence search problems seem rather arbitrary; i.e., the loss functions used in each of these problem setups seem arbitrary. Thus, while these are valid examples of how the framework could be used to derive AFs for non-standard choices of $\ell$ and $\mathcal{A}$, their practical relevance is not evident. The authors should clarify whether these problem setups (and their corresponding choices of $\ell$) have been considered in the literature before.

3. The loss function used for the level set estimation problem is odd. A more appropriate measure of performance for this problem setup is the F1-score (see, e.g., Gotovos et al (2013). Active learning for level set estimation).

4. The numerical experiments that consider level set estimation problems should include AFs tailored for that particular task. One example is the LSE acquisition function from Gotovos et al (2013).

5. It is a bit disappointing that a novel H-entropy search AF for the standard BO setting is not proposed. It would be interesting to explore other choices of $\ell$ and $\mathcal{A}$ in this setting.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work introduces an interesting class of AFs which is shown to contain many of the existing AFs in standard BO as special cases. While this unified view is interesting, its usefulness is not clearly demonstrated. In particular, the practical relevance of the special cases of $\ell$ and $\mathcal{A}$ considered in this paper is not evident. Moreover, the empirical evaluation does not consider existing acquisition functions tailored for the level set estimation problem, and thus does not demonstrate competitiveness with respect to the current state-of-the-art. In general, there is a substantial amount of work to do to prove that such a unified view could be useful.

content.title: Response to Reviewer QqKr
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments and feedback. We will use these to improve the quality of our paper. We respond back to your comments below.

### **Benefits of our framework:**
We think you bring up a nice discussion on the topic of *why* it is beneficial to develop our framework, which both unifies existing acquisition functions (EI, ES/PES, KG), and can specialize to tasks beyond standard optimization.

Our main motivation in developing this framework was for the following reasons:
1. It is often unclear which of the existing acquisition functions to use in a given run of BO; our framework provides explicit guidance of when it is more optimal to choose e.g. EI vs ES/PES vs KG, depending on a user’s goals, and the loss that they care about (see “Practical guidance and summary” in Section 4).
2. Our framework allows for easily and automatically deriving one-step-optimal acquisition procedures for *new* optimization problems given a specific user-provided loss (and we demonstrate this on three example tasks).
3. Our framework allows for gradient-based acquisition optimization methods on a wide set of tasks—both for new acquisition functions, as well as on existing acquisition functions such as KG/ES (and this in turn can yield new procedures for existing BO acquisition functions, as described below).

We will state these reasons more explicitly in an updated draft of our paper.

### **Gradient-based acquisition optimization for KG, EI:**
We want to clarify what we believe is a misconception here: the gradient-based acquisition optimization in our framework can indeed apply to both knowledge gradient (KG) and entropy search (ES) acquisition functions. In fact, all KG results in our paper used our gradient-based implementation (we have now stated this explicitly in the updated version of our paper). This is because, for KG, the action space and domain are both continuous, and the loss is differentiable.

While we did not show results on ES, our framework can apply here as well, if we parameterize the action space (which is a space of distributions in the case of ES, as shown in Equation (5)) with a real vector (i.e. distribution reparameterization). We think that this would be an interesting direction to explore further in future work.

### **Loss function in top-k, sequence search, and LSE tasks:**
Our primary goal of these experiments was to show that we can easily and automatically take any user- or problem-defined loss, and produce a performant acquisition function for that loss. While you may feel that these losses are not the best for a given task, this is not our main argument here. We do, however, think that these losses are reasonable solutions to the given tasks at hand, and that they provide a nice demonstration of the goals of our framework.
We also want to clarify that the specific losses are indeed new, though the broad problems themselves (such as top-$k$ estimation, level set estimation, etc.) are not novel; we will update our draft with references to these papers. We will also add a citation/discussion on Gotovos et al (2013)—thank you for the reference— which provides another nice loss for LSE, which could be approached by our framework.

### **Novel acquisition function for vanilla optimization:**
We agree that this is an interesting direction to pursue—to derive a new acquisition function for *standard* optimization, based on an alternative loss/action set. However, the main reason we did not focus on this in our paper was because (1) there already seem to exist many good acquisition functions for this task, and so we wanted to focus on the ability of our framework to handle new problems/losses, and (2) we wanted to show how our framework can shed light on the relations between existing BO acquisition functions, and provide guidance on selecting among them (see bullet #1 above).

content.title: Thank you for your response and follow up
content.comment:
Dear authors,

I would like to thank you for your response. Most of my concerns remain, so I would like to follow up with the questions/comments below.

1. There is value in using well-motivated choices of $(\ell,  \mathcal{A})$ in your examples as this would make the significance of your contribution more evident. In particular, it would be helpful to include an example where $(\ell,  \mathcal{A})$ has been previously considered in the literature, but where the implied acquisition function has not been used so far and, hopefully, improves over the state of the art.

2. Thank you for clarifying that the conditions required to prove differentiability are satisfied by KG and ES. At the same time, while looking at this result more carefully, I realized that several conditions are necessary to guarantee that either the gradient descent or SAA optimization approaches are reasonable. When using the former, for example, one needs to guarantee that the variance of the stochastic estimator is bounded, which is not true in general (see, e.g., Wang et al. (2016). Parallel Bayesian global optimization of expensive functions). For the latter, it would be desirable to derive conditions under which the approximate solutions converge to a true solution as the number of samples increases (i.e., a result along the lines of Theorem 1 in Balandat et al. (2020)). Finally, I would like to point out that the SAA approach is quite computationally demanding as the size of the optimization domain increases exponentially with the number of samples.  It would be helpful to discuss how many samples were used in your experiments and also include runtimes.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper generalizes standard Bayesian optimization techniques for optimizing an unknown target function to a greedy strategy called H-entropy search for minimizing a decision-loss associated with the unknown target function.
content.main_review:
This paper considers optimizing a decision loss for an unkown target function by querying values of the function in a Bayesian framework. A greedy strategy (called H-entropy search) is proposed - it queries the example leading to maximum reduction in the posterior expected Bayes risk. It is shown to be a generalization of the standard Bayesian techniques for optimizing an unknown target function. It is shown that when the loss function associated with the posterior Bayes risk satisfies certain mild conditions, the greedy strategy can be conveniently implemented via gradient-based optimization. The greedy strategy is applied to several optimization problems by designing problem-specific losses: top-k estimation with diversity, generalized level set estimation and multi-value sequence search. For these problems, the greedy strategy outperforms several baseline approach, which is unsurprising as those baseline approaches are not designed to minimize the problem-specific loss functions. 

The paper is well-written and easy to read. The experiments demonstrates that the greedy approach outperforms several baselines which do not take the decision loss into account during information gathering. The idea is natural and simple, but it is interesting to see that several standard Bayesian optimization techniques can be seen as special cases of the greedy approach (though proofs are straigtforward), and this general framework may find broad applications.

To strenghthen the paper, it would be helpful to address the following questions for the experiments so as to provide a more complete picture of the performance of the proposed algortihm:
- During test time, is the predicted action the posterior Bayes action? In particular, how is a point classified for level set estimation?
- Are GP priors used in all the experiments? If yes, how are the kernels and hyperparameters chosen?
- For tok-k estimation, how do the plots of the sum of the selected inputs against iteration look like?
- Is vanilla stochastic gradient descent used to for computing the acquisition function in the greedy algorithm? If yes, how is the learning rate chosen? In addition, what is the sample size used in computing gradient estimates?
- How much time does each iteration take for each method?

Minor comments
- Proposition 2: $P(\Theta)$ need to be replaced by all possible distributions on ${\cal X}$.
- What do PES and MES stand for? Are they just alternative names for ES (entropy search)?
- pp. 5: optimiztion -> optimization
- pp. 7: "for this task the Vaccination function" -> for the Vaccination function
content.summary_of_the_review: A simple and natural idea that is clearly explained and supported by experiments. The idea potentially has broad applications for minimizing a decision-loss associated with an unknown target function.

content.title: Response to Reviewer jUAT
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable comments and feedback, which we will use to improve our paper. We address each of your comments below.

### **Evaluation for level set estimation:**
For evaluation in our level set estimation experiment, we use the posterior mean to produce an estimate of the level for each point in our domain, and then use these estimates to compute the accuracy metrics that are shown in Figure 2. We have clarified this detail in our paper.

### **GP priors, kernels, and hyperparameters:**
In all experiments, we use a GP prior with squared exponential (RBF) kernel as our prior model. Hyperparameters for this model are fit at each iteration of our procedure by maximizing the marginal log-likelihood.

### **Gradient descent:**
We use gradient descent (full batch, non-stochastic gradient descent) to optimize the acquisition function at each iteration of our procedure. We use a constant learning rate of 0.1 for all experiments—though we note that more sophisticated optimization routines and learning rate schedules could be used within our method, if desired.

### **Timing of each method:**
We will add timing results to our paper. As an example, we performed a timing study on the top-k estimation problem, and our method takes between 3s and 10s per iteration (depending on the stage of the trial and number of observations). This is similar to the time taken by baselines such as knowledge gradient (KG).

### **Top-k estimation:**
Note that our goal in this task is to optimize (roughly speaking) the regularized sum of the top-k estimated points at each iteration—we assume this is what is meant in the comment about showing “the sum of the selected inputs”. (Note also that we need diversity-regularization in our loss so that the top-k points do not degenerate to a single point). Given this, we do indeed show iteration versus the *regularized sum of the top-k points versus iteration* in our paper in Figure 1 (where the negative loss in this case is this sum, as defined by Equation (7)).

### **PES and MES:**
PES stands for predictive entropy search, and MES stands for max-value entropy search. We have updated our paper draft to define these acronyms when they are first introduced.

content.title: Thank you for your suggestions and comments
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their valuable feedback on this paper.

As a brief summary, our paper aims to provide a family of acquisition functions based on a decision-theoretic generalization of entropy. Our framework can both recover/unify existing acquisition functions used in Bayesian optimization (which we prove for expected improvement, knowledge gradient, and entropy search methods), and allow for automatic construction of new acquisition functions tailored to a given user-specified loss, for new/custom sequential decision making tasks. It also allows for an efficient gradient-based acquisition optimization method that can apply to a broad set of acquisition functions derived under this framework.

The reviewers have brought up a few points that we agree would make the paper stronger, including:
- Clarification about the high-level goals and benefits of our framework.
- Updates to the explanation and definition of the generalized decision-theoretic entropy.
- Adjustments to experiments and addition of experimental details.

We prefer to make these updates in order to allow for a stronger presentation, and then resubmit the paper for re-evaluation. We will therefore withdraw the current submission.
